> Dear Frank,
>
>
>
> *TL;DR:* The edgecov() terms are very memory-inefficient. I don't know
> what these mg/m4/mt matrices represent, but if they can be generated from,
> say, nodal information, you can implement a custom ergm term that gets
> passed nodal information and generates them on the fly.
>
>
>
> *Technical explanation: *Internally, ergm concatenates covariate vectors
> and passes them on to the C code, where they get unpacked. Each edgecov()
> term passes an n*n matrix, and in your case, each of these matrices is
> 270000^2 elements long. Three of them add up to a vector of length
> 2187000000 <%28218%29%20700-0000> which is longer than the greatest
> integer that can be represented using the basic integer type (2147483647
> <%28214%29%20748-3647>). Now, R can handle vectors like that, but not
> through the .C() interface.
>
>
>
> I hope this helps,
>
> Pavel
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet community,

I?m quite new to network analysis, so I apologize in advance for any inconsistencies. And the lengthy email :)

I?m building thousands of networks of conversations, and I have a couple of questions about how to build them/calculate some relevant statistics:

1. First, I tried two different approaches to building these networks. One is to build a list of network objects, so that each conversation has its independent network. Each conversation is built from a subset of the full edgelist identified by a specific conversation ID (this is added to the edgelist as a third column). The problem with this approach may be that the list becomes extremely big.

The second approach is to build a single large network object g from which later on subgraphs will be obtained iteratively by accessing only the subset of edges identified with a specific id, which I previously added as an edge attribute

get.inducedSubgraph(g, eid = which(g%e%"my_convo"== convo)

but I eventually want to be able to calculate network statistics independently for each conversation, and with this second method I?m not sure whether a given subgraph would be assessed independently should one (or more) of its nodes be also part of other subgraphs (given that it is possible that one actor could have participated in many conversations).

Which method should I follow, and are there any other considerations I haven?t thought of?

2. Since I?m working with conversational data, it is often the case that two nodes start a mutual exchange within a thread, creating redundant ties. This is actually very meaningful information that I would like to consider when  calculating several network measures. Once again, I?ve taken two approaches: one, I have built the network from the weighted edgelist mentioned above. It would look something like this:



In this case, only unique edges will be counted (7) on the network summary, and weight is an edge attribute. 

The second approach is to build the network with an edgelist containing redundant ties. The above case would then look like:

user6	user7	5
user6	user7	5
user6	user7	5
?
user7	user6	5
user7	user6	5
?

and so on. A summary of this network will count all edges (24). So the approach I take changes how some measures are going to be calculated and ought to be interpreted. I?ve looked online and it seems that reciprocity and density are not very reliable measures for weighted networks. How should one proceed when such redundancies actually matter and should be taken into account when evaluating, for example, the overall level of reciprocity in a conversation?

Thank you so much for any help; looking forward to reading your answers.
Sincerely,
Teresa

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Teresa -

If you have a very large collection of sparse dyadic networks without 
much meta-data (e.g., individual attributes), you may find it easiest to 
store them as a list of sna edgelists (see the help in the sna package 
for more details).? They are simple, lean, can encode values, and can be 
interconverted into other forms if needed.? If you need a richer format, 
lists of network objects (which you have considered previously) are 
often very effective; if you only have thousands of networks, then the 
length of the list should not be a concern.? (It could be a problem if 
you have more than, say, 1e8 conversations.? But that's probably not the 
case.)

In terms of encoding numbers of contacts between pairs, storing this as 
a value associated with each edge will probably prove easiest for most 
conventional network analyses.? That said, if you are really interested 
in things like conversational interaction then you are probably not 
interested in conventional network analysis - you are really looking at 
relational event sequences.? Rather than trying to find a way to 
shoehorn your question into a network analytic framework, you might want 
to consider an approach that considers such a process on its own terms 
(e.g. a REM model or sequence analysis).? That said, there are lots of 
things that can be learned by "flattening" an interaction sequence 
across time and treating it as an aggregated network, and I find that to 
be a useful exploratory step in such analyses; there's no single 
approach that answers all questions.

Anyway, hope that helps!

There are lots of things that you can do with hypergraphs in statnet, but

can.?The question is, "what do you want to do with hypergraphs that you

Hi, Meredith -

Based on your description, it sounds like those edge variables should be 
structural 0s, not NAs.? (NA would mean that you don't know the value of 
the edge.? A structural 0 is a null that is fixed by something exogenous 
to the network generating process. Since the monkeys here could not have 
interacted, you would want - if I understand your situation correctly - 
to treat those cells as structural 0s.)? To do that, you will want to 
leave the network as is (i.e., set the edges as absent, not missing) and 
use the constraints argument to ergm() to tell the model that those 
edges are constrained to be absent; see the constraints help page for 
details on how to do that.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

Hi, Meredith -

Based on your description, it sounds like those edge variables should be
structural 0s, not NAs.  (NA would mean that you don't know the value of
the edge.  A structural 0 is a null that is fixed by something exogenous to
the network generating process.  Since the monkeys here could not have
interacted, you would want - if I understand your situation correctly - to
treat those cells as structural 0s.)  To do that, you will want to leave
the network as is (i.e., set the edges as absent, not missing) and use the
constraints argument to ergm() to tell the model that those edges are
constrained to be absent; see the constraints help page for details on how
to do that.

Hi, Meredith,

This is because that constraint combination is not implemented in the current ergm and ergm.count releases. There are two options:
1) If you are comfortable installing packages from GitHub (https://github.com/statnet/ergm), a pre-release version implements it.

I hope this helps,
Pavel
